title: Modeling and controlling a half-car model suspension system using an ANFIS controller
content:
by Sisay Ewunetie Fisha, Amanuel Gebisa Aga, Tatek Mamo Wachamo

Passive suspension systems (PSS) use fixed spring and damping characteristics and cannot adapt to changing road disturbances and operating conditions. Active suspension systems (ASS) address this limitation by generating additional control forces, but controller design must balance ride comfort, road holding, model uncertainty, and control effort. This study develops a four-degree-of-freedom (4-DOF) longitudinal half-car model and evaluates an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) controller against PSS and PID-controlled ASS under double-bump and ISO-classified random Type A and Type C Road profiles at 10 and 20 m/s. The ANFIS controller is trained using PID-generated input-output data with two inputs, five Gaussian membership functions per input, 25 Takagi-Sugeno rules, and 150 training epochs. For the double-bump case at 10 m/s, ANFIS reduces body vertical displacement from 0.0435 to 0.0084 m (80.6%), vertical acceleration from 2.40 to 0.77 m/s2 (67.9%), and front suspension travel from 0.0652 to 0.0090 m (86.2%) relative to PSS. Compared with PID, the corresponding reductions are 53.6%, 49.3%, and 43.8%, respectively. Settling time is reduced by 38.8% for body vertical displacement and 38.6% for pitch acceleration relative to PSS. The result meets all the qualifications for riding comfort of the ISO 2631 standard. The study identifies limitations related to PID-supervised training, linear modeling, and actuator-energy assessment by employing simulation. Experimental evaluation is required to establish robustness to parameter uncertainty, sensor noise, actuator delay, and implementation energy requirements.
